share_verdict: Acid-set curd and rice flour. No khoya, no maida.
translation: Milk split with takra-maṇḍa, the curd drained and bound with rice flour, shaped, fried in ghee and soaked in sugar syrup, scented with cardamom.

ingredients.name: milk, split with takra-maṇḍa
ingredients.function: takra-maṇḍa is the thin whey drawn off curd — a gentle coagulant. Modern kitchens use lemon juice, vinegar or citric acid, all of which are harsher and genuinely change the curd's texture

ingredients.name: rice flour
ingredients.function: the binder. Not maida, and not khoya

ingredients.name: cardamom
ingredients.function: the only aromatic — no rose, no saffron

method_reconstructed: Split the milk with takra-maṇḍa, the thin whey from the previous day's curd.
Drain the curd and bind it with rice flour.
Shape, fry in ghee, and soak in cardamom sugar syrup.
contested_points: The coagulant is the ingredient worth actually testing: takra-maṇḍa gives a softer, grainier curd than lemon or vinegar, and the texture difference is real rather than nominal.
The result is grainy-soft and faintly lactic, not the melting-soft khoya jamun of today; chhena murki is arguably the closer living relative.

changed.from: acid-set milk curd bound with rice flour
changed.driver: roller-milled refined flour and commercially reduced khoya both became cheap and standard, and they give the melting texture the modern sweet is judged on

changed.to: lemon juice, vinegar or citric acid
changed.driver: faster and more reliable, and available off a shelf — but harsher on the curd

changed.from: cardamom alone, eaten within the meal
changed.to: cardamom, rose and saffron, eaten as dessert
changed.driver: rosewater and saffron entered the sweet repertoire, and the course moved to the end of the meal

ingredients: 1 cup thin whey from yesterday's curd (or well-diluted buttermilk) as the coagulant
Sugar syrup with 4 cardamom pods — no rose, no saffron
steps: Heat the milk and split it with the whey rather than lemon. It curdles more slowly and the curd comes out softer.
Drain in a cloth, then knead with rice flour until it binds.
Shape small, fry gently in ghee — hot fat will crack them.
Grainy-soft and faintly lactic rather than melting. Higher in milk protein and lower in refined starch than a khoya-and-maida jamun.

verification.note: Passage located and rendered in the editorial extraction, dated 1129 CE, including the takra-maṇḍa coagulant note. Devanagari not yet transcribed into this record.
